To despise the people of Heaven.
To disturb the governance of the state.
To reward what is unrighteous.
To punish the innocent.
To kill persons in order to seize their wealth.
To ruin others in order to seize their positions.
To slaughter those who surrender and to put to death those who submit.
To demote the upright and push aside the worthy.
To oppress the orphaned and coerce the widowed.
To cast aside the law and accept bribes.
To take the straight for the crooked, and the crooked for the straight.
To make light cases into heavy ones.
To look upon an execution and add to the fury.
To know one’s faults yet not reform.
To see what is good yet not do it.
To draw others into one’s own guilt.
To dam up the arts of healing.
To mock and slander sages and worthies.
To encroach upon and insult persons of virtue.
To shoot at what flies and pursue what runs.
To disturb hibernating creatures and startle roosting ones.
To fill up burrows and overturn nests.
To harm the embryo and break the egg.
To wish that others suffer loss.
To destroy the successes of others.
To endanger others in order to secure one’s own ease.
To diminish others in order to benefit oneself.
To trade the good for the bad.
To discard the public for the sake of the private.
To steal the abilities of others.
To conceal the goodness of others.
To expose the ugliness of others.
To lay bare the private affairs of others.
To waste the goods and wealth of others.
To separate others from their own flesh and blood.
To intrude upon what others cherish.
To help others in doing wrong.
To give rein to one’s will and wield tyrannical power.
To humiliate others in order to seek victory.
To ruin the crops of others.
To break up the marriages of others.
To grow rich in an unjust way and then act haughtily.
To escape punishment through luck and be without shame.
To claim others’ kindness as one’s own and push one’s faults onto them.
To shift calamity onto others and sell away one’s own wrongdoing.
To buy and peddle an empty reputation.
To harbor a sinister heart.
To cut down what others are skilled at.
To shelter one’s own shortcomings.
To avail oneself of power to coerce and threaten.
To unleash cruelty, killing and harming.
To cut and tailor without cause.
To cook and slaughter in a manner contrary to what is proper.
To scatter and discard the five grains.
To exhaust and disturb the multitude of living beings.
To ruin the families of others and take their wealth and treasures.
To breach the waters and set fires, in order to harm the dwellings of the people.
To throw the plans and schemes of others into confusion, in order to spoil their accomplishments.
To damage the tools and vessels of others, in order to make their use difficult.
To see others honored and noble, and wish them banished and deposed.
To see others wealthy, and wish them ruined and scattered.
To see the beauty of others, and harbor the thought of possessing them.
To owe others goods and wealth, and wish them dead.
When one’s solicitations are not granted, to straightway give rise to cursing and hatred.
To see others lose their advantage, and then speak of their faults.
To see that the bodies of others are not whole, and laugh at them.
To see that the talents of others are worthy of praise, and suppress them.
To bury talismans and practice dark sorcery to curse others.
To use drugs to kill trees.
To bear rage and anger against one’s teacher.
To offend and rebel against one’s father and elder brother.
An Annotated, Explained, and Case-Assembled Plain-Language Abridged Edition of the Tract of the Most Exalted One on Retribution, Volume Three
[Explanation]
When a wicked person becomes an official, far from loving the state and its people, he even dares to act capriciously in despising and bullying the people of the world.
[Analysis]

Emperor Taizong of the Tang said: ‘The people are the foundation of the state, and virtue is the foundation of being human; if a person’s virtue is deeply accumulated, then he will be remembered and admired forever, and if the people can live in peace and contentment, then the state will naturally be secure and firm.’ Therefore, if a ruler has deep and generous virtue, then the people will turn to him just as they turn to their own parents! When we observe the sage-kings of ancient and modern times, at home and abroad, they all loved the people and cherished all things, regarding the people as if they were wounded, and caring for the common people as they would care for their own children. How much more should the officials who govern provinces and counties on behalf of the ruler embody this principle!
Story One:

Zheng Qingchen of the Song dynasty was by nature exceedingly cruel and ungrateful. When he served as magistrate of Huaili County, he mistreated the people of the county; and when his term of office ended and he was leaving, the people of Huaili County crowded and blocked the road, and spat and cursed at him. Zheng Qingchen then reported to the court that the people under his jurisdiction had insulted a superior official. Emperor Zhenzong of the Song said: ‘The most important thing in governing is to win the hearts of the people. Since the people have so utterly rejected and rebelled against your administration, then what you did and what you failed to do in Huaili County can be known without even asking! You even dare to complain, reporting to the court that the people insulted you in public — this is indeed brazen and outrageous!’ Zheng Qingchen was therefore convicted by the court and demoted.
Story Two:

In the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, because of the frost damage in autumn, the crops were severely harmed. The emperor, concerned about the disaster, ordered the provinces and counties to investigate the extent of the crop damage within their jurisdictions and report it to the court. But Liu Zao, the magistrate of Weinan County in Shaanxi, reported to the court: ‘The crops in my county have not suffered any damage at all!’ Because reports of damage were coming in from all over while Weinan County alone reported no damage, the emperor became very suspicious and sent someone to investigate. It turned out that the damaged crop area in Weinan County exceeded three thousand qing. When the emperor heard the investigation report, he sighed and said: ‘A magistrate is the parent-official of the people. Even if the county under his jurisdiction had suffered no disaster, he should still have said that it had suffered damage. Magistrate Liu Zao is indeed so inhumane!’ Therefore the emperor convicted Liu Zao and banished him to a far-off place.
When a wicked person becomes an official, not only can he not love the state and its people, he actually disturbs the governance of the state and disrupts the order of society!

A state must nurture the blessings of peace and must not arbitrarily alter its laws and institutions; even when there are projects to be undertaken or reforms to be made, they must be considered with great care and deliberation. If it is merely the private intent of one person to make changes, and he rashly proposes reforms, then with every measure implemented there will be corresponding disturbance and harm. Moreover, the laws and regulations established by the ancestors, which officials at all levels have administered for a very long time, and to which the people have grown accustomed and found convenient — why must they be repeatedly altered, merely to disturb the governance of the state?

When Li Hang of the Song dynasty was chief minister, Ma Liang said to Li Hang: ‘Among the outside world’s criticisms of your administration, many consider that you accomplish nothing.’ Li Hang replied: ‘I have no particular talent for handling the affairs of the state; but among the proposals on the benefits and harms of affairs at home and abroad, whenever the recommendations for change overflow with impatience and agitation, I do not adopt them. The reason I do this is that I wish to replenish the vital energy of the state! Today the laws and regulations of the state may be said to be as many as the hairs on an ox; if I follow their recommendations and implement them one by one, then it will cause much harm to the state and the people!’ Those officials who harbor unkind intentions, wanting to seize the opportunity to distinguish themselves and claim credit — how would they be willing to consider that doing so might disturb the people!

The Tang chief minister Li Linfu promoted the method of the fengqi conscripted cavalry; and the great ministers of the court debated this proposal of Li Linfu, with many taking an opposing stance. But Li Linfu stubbornly insisted on his own opinion, and the defensive strength of the Tang dynasty was never restored after the implementation of the fengqi method. Wang Anshi, the chief minister of the Song dynasty, instituted the new laws, and even stubbornly and hastily enforced them; as a result, he brought great distress to the people, so that the vitality of the Song state was greatly harmed by the implementation of the new laws, and the national strength declined with extreme rapidity. These are all the harmful consequences of disturbing the governance of the state!
To be unable to reward the good and punish the evil, so as to manifest the function of encouraging good and warning against evil, and instead go so far as to reward the unrighteous and wicked.

The principle of rewarding is precisely to honor virtue and repay merit, so ‘reward’ is an important institution of the state and court for encouraging and exhorting the people. To reward what should not be rewarded is called unrighteous. Thus, to go against right and wrong, to abandon the law and discipline, to encourage evil conduct, to be partial and selfish, to employ the wicked and replace the good — these measures most provoke the wrath of Heaven! So those responsible for rank and reward — can they fail to be careful?
Story:

In the Zhou dynasty, Duke Wen of Jin had a close attendant who had followed him in exile and shared his hardships, who said to him: ‘Among the three kinds of rewards you, the king, have conferred, none has been given to me, your humble servant! It must be that I, your humble servant, bear some fault, and so it is that I come to you to beg to be punished.’ Duke Wen of Jin said: ‘He who guides me with benevolence and righteousness, and exhorts me with virtue and kindness, receives my highest reward; he who assists me and helps me succeed in carrying out benevolent governance, receives my middle reward; he who shares my hardships, shedding blood and sweat and being wounded to protect my safety, receives my third reward. As for one who merely serves me with his physical labor and does nothing to help me correct my shortcomings, his reward comes only after the three kinds of reward have been bestowed; so today you will receive this kind of reward.’ When the people of Jin heard Duke Wen of Jin speak and act in this way regarding rewards, they were all overjoyed.
[Further Analysis]

Duke Wen of Jin’s rewards may be said to have been in accord with righteousness, and this was also an important reason why Duke Wen of Jin was able to dominate the feudal lords. If one achieves rewarding in accord with righteousness, then how could there be even the slightest negligence in bestowing a single rank or office, a single thread of silk or a single grain of rice upon the state? In this way, naturally, those who scheme, toady, flatter and send gifts can no longer prevail; while those who uphold the law, fulfill their duties and work seriously will all exhort and encourage one another, and render meritorious service to the state and society.
To inflict punishment upon innocent good people, causing them to bear injustice and suffer wrongs.

The purpose of punishment is to punish and warn the wicked; the sage could not help but establish punishment. Therefore punishment is by nature not auspicious, nor is it a good thing; and when the measure of the punishment and the crime committed by the offender are commensurate, one should still pity and commiserate with them, for they fell into the net of the law because they did not understand the principles. One must not rejoice because a case was solved and a merit was gained, for this may lead to an error in the case! Therefore the ancients were very careful in weighing punishment, and investigated and examined in meticulous detail. If the punishment is inappropriate, causing the innocent to suffer harm, then not only is it an unfair and flawed review of the case, it also violates the gracious intention of Heaven’s love of life! Moreover, the law is explicit that one who kills must die. If today, through one’s own negligence and error, one punishes the innocent, more than one person is killed, and the retribution to be borne by only one person — then how can the principle of a life for a life be made fair? Alas! For this kind of offense, even a normally upright and incorruptible official may, at a time when the case is beset with doubt and suspicion or the evidence is ambiguous, stubbornly insist on his own opinion in deciding the crime, without the humility to investigate carefully; and so end up with lifelong regret and remorse. Moreover, the innocent who were killed will certainly repay wrong with wrong and pursue relentlessly! How much more severe is the retribution for those officials who are careless in reviewing cases! Thinking of this, can one not be afraid?

When Ma Bing served as magistrate of Jiayu County, a river bandit leader with his followers dared to storm into the government office, set a fire, looted the official silver and then made off. The ringleader of these bandits had a very long beard. After the Jiayu County office was plundered, news happened to arrive saying that a boat at Tuanfeng Town was carrying over a dozen people who behaved quite suspiciously, one of whom had a long beard and was likely the bandit leader — but in fact he was not. Ma Bing nevertheless ordered the arrest of this person, and even publicized the breaking of the case. This unfortunate man, wrongly mistaken for the river bandit, was thrown into prison after his arrest and died an unjust death in jail. Later, when Ma Bing was promoted and became a censor, the real bandits were captured by another county office; and the head of that office happened to be a former colleague of Ma Bing, so he did not pursue this wrongful case. Later Ma Bing was promoted again and became chief censor. One time the boat he took happened to pass Tuanfeng Town, and that night they moored there to pass the night. Unexpectedly, that night they were robbed by bandits, and the whole family of Ma Bing was killed by the bandits.

In the past there was an official surnamed Yan who, when serving as governor of Nanjing, was told by someone that a resident of Zhenjiang named Zhou Zhilian was the leader of the bandits. Zhou Zhilian was thus summoned to the Nanjing office and subjected to interrogation and investigation. Zhou Zhilian’s family was wealthy and his life comfortable, and in his heart he greatly feared that the office would subject him to torture to extort a confession, so he found a way to bribe the powerful and influential to speak on his behalf. Therefore Governor Yan became even more suspicious of Zhou Zhilian, and actually had him beaten to death with a staff. Governor Yan later died, having his life taken by the vengeful spirit of Zhou Zhilian.

Governor Yan, suspecting that Zhou Zhilian had bribed [someone] and killing him, seems on the surface to be quite just. However, killing a person who had not committed a capital offense could still turn him into a fierce ghost to take revenge and demand his life. From this case one may know that whoever is an official must not presume that he is impartial and selfless, and can then arbitrarily and recklessly decide to condemn people to death!
Story Three:

Li Guizheng served as a judge and had been deciding cases for a very long time. One day, when he had business to attend to and was going out, passing over Sanjing Bridge, he personally saw more than a dozen people with disheveled hair, shouting loudly: ‘We have been wronged — we were wrongfully killed!’ They gradually approached and pressed upon him. Li Guizheng became extremely frightened, and immediately turned back home. After returning home, he admonished his son, saying: ‘When you study to become an official, never take up the task of hearing cases and judging the guilt of people! I served as a judge, and because I was incorruptible, cautious and fearful, I often followed precedent to pass judgment, and so wrongfully killed so many people. Even though I repent today, it is already too late!’ Not long after, Li Guizheng died.

Even a judge as incorruptible, cautious and fearful as Li Guizheng could make a wrong judgment and kill the wrong person. Then as for those judges who are neither incorruptible, nor cautious, nor fearful — when they see Li Guizheng’s fate, one wonders whether they will be stirred to vigilance!
To intentionally kill persons and take their wealth.

Killing a person to seize the wealth of the dead — such wicked conduct is not necessarily done only by bandits. For example, greedy and corrupt officials, in order to covet wealth that is not rightfully theirs, use the means of punishment to kill suspects in prison. The wealthy and powerful, insatiably greedy, may push those who owe them money — even when these people are reduced to penury and wander in distress — these wealthy families nevertheless, against their conscience, press them to repay within a deadline and even add heavy interest. Cruel and ruthless people, in order to covet wealth, actually take advantage of others’ peril to seize their wealth, without the least concern for others’ lives. Unscrupulous doctors covet wealth, disregard the lives of their patients, and exploit the critical condition of the sick to squeeze money out of them. All these people, because of coveting wealth, conceive the intention to kill and carry out the act of killing! Yet none of those who kill for wealth fails to be killed by a vengeful ghost demanding his life; and the wealth they plundered all turns into nothing in the end!

Along the Yangtze River there was a boatman named Gong Zhuan. Taking advantage of a great wind rising on the river, he pushed a wealthy merchant into the water and drowned him; then he seized the money left on the boat by the merchant. Because of this Gong Zhuan turned into a rich man and settled in Weiyang. Before long, his wife bore him a son; and when this son grew up, for some unknown reason he regarded his father as an enemy. Gong Zhuan was greatly enraged, and went to a temple to inquire of the planchette spirit. The spirit said: ‘In the eighth month of the gengzi year, the west wind was fierce; waves rose in the Yangtze River. Twenty years ago a single mistaken thought — I beg you, sir, to feel your own heart!’ Gong Zhuan was greatly startled, and knew that the wealthy merchant — whom he had pushed into the water and drowned in the Yangtze River twenty years earlier — had already been reborn as his son to take revenge upon him! So Gong Zhuan fled his home in terror, and in the end died an unnatural death.

From this one may know that any wealth obtained through scheming, one definitely cannot rest easy in enjoying it, for it will still be taken over by the resentful foe one has wronged; and what one gains for oneself is twenty years of living in fear and trepidation, and ultimately dying a bad death. Moreover, the judges of the underworld have not yet settled accounts with one; if the reckoning is made in the underworld, the torment would be even more unbearable to hear of!

In the past there was a yamen runner. One early morning he set out from home very early, and as he passed through the desolate wilderness, he was seen by an outsider who carried valuables with him. When this outsider saw the runner approaching with his weapon, he feared the runner might harbor ill intent toward him, so he immediately hid in the grass. The runner was then uncertain, and only heard a rustling sound from the grass; not seeing anyone nearby, he feared that a tiger or leopard might be hiding in the grass. So he thrust his long spear randomly into the grass, and struck the outsider. When he dragged him out of the grass, the man was already dead. The runner then realized that he had killed the man by accident. With no other recourse, he took the valuables the outsider carried, and discarded the corpse in the grass. This matter was never discovered. The runner thereby became rich, and his wife gave birth to a daughter. One day, at his gate, the runner suddenly saw the outsider whom he had accidentally stabbed to death. He immediately shut the gate and hid behind it to peek; the outsider actually entered the home of the cobbler across the street. Before long, the cobbler’s wife bore a son. The runner knew the karmic link and treated the cobbler very well, doting on and loving the cobbler’s son. When his own daughter grew up, he prepared to marry her to the cobbler’s son. The cobbler was overjoyed and asked his son to honor and care for the runner, just as he would his own father. One summer, the weather was very hot, and the runner, having drunk himself tipsy, lay asleep on the bed; his sweat kept seeping out. The cobbler’s son, attending him at his side, took a knife and gently scraped away the sweat on the runner’s body. Because the runner was drunk and befuddled, he felt something moving about on his body, and struck at it with his hand; so the knife went askew and stabbed into the runner’s belly. At that point the runner was not yet dead, so he called his family and told them the truth of the matter, immediately married his daughter to the cobbler’s son, and returned all the family property to him.
To frame others in order to seize their official positions.

Every rank and office in the world, though settled by destiny, can be attained if a subordinate is willing to endeavor to abandon evil and cultivate virtue, for he may be promoted to a very eminent position. An ordinary person so long as he does many good deeds also has a chance of obtaining rank and emolument. But if, in order to advance oneself, one stops at nothing to frame others so as to seize their positions — then because the cycle of cause and effect is clear and Heaven’s justice is manifest, the one who frames others will in the end be framed by others; and the one who seizes others’ positions will in the end have his own position taken away by others. Moreover, the retribution is so swift that it can almost be seen at once!

Mi Dechao, a great minister of the Song dynasty, seeing that the merit and prestige of the Grand Councilor Cao Bin were growing daily more prominent, framed Cao Bin before the emperor as secretly plotting treason and intending to rebel. The emperor, believing the slander of Mi Dechao, dismissed Cao Bin from office and promoted Mi Dechao to the important post of Grand Councilor. Not long after this happened, Chief Minister Zhao Pu did his utmost to defend Cao Bin and clear his name. The emperor finally came to his senses, and banished Mi Dechao to a very far place, while treating Cao Bin with the same honor as before. Seeing this story, is it not all the more clear that to frame others is to frame oneself? And yet such harm is still considered minor! As for Li Linfu, the chief minister of the Tang dynasty, who repeatedly framed others to secure his own position — at that time the marshals of the frontier were all renowned ministers of the court; those with outstanding merit could enter the court and become chief ministers. Li Linfu wanted to block this path to the premiership, so he said to the emperor: ‘Civil officials are timid and dare not resist the invasion of foreign troops; if one employs barbarians to serve as marshals, the barbarians will surely fight to the death to protect the great Tang.’ The emperor, misled, adopted Li Linfu’s suggestion. This led to the rebellion of An Lushan and the great chaos under heaven. This is an example of how the selfish thought of preserving one’s own rank and emolument caused havoc among the people of the world. In the end, Li Linfu was convicted by the court of colluding in treason, and even after death his coffin was opened and his corpse beheaded — a crime he had not committed! Yet because he framed the worthy to secure his own position and thereby employed An Lushan, so the court attached the crime of treason to him — is this not the case freely settled by Heaven in the unseen realm? Alas! One who enjoys the ruler’s salary, and serves as his minister, should repay the ruler and the state; how can he commit such deeds that defy Heaven and reason!
[Words of Worth]

The ancients said: ‘Since one has entrusted oneself to serve the ruler, then this body should no longer be one’s own; so one should think of the ruler and the state in every thought. How can one still attend to one’s own life and family? Would such a minister not be loyal to the state?’ These words of the ancients may truly serve as words of precious advice for the persons mentioned above!
When bandits have already surrendered and submitted, to instead kill them most greatly defies the principle of Heaven.

War is an inauspicious thing; combat is truly perilous, and the sage resorted to arms only when he could not help it. Therefore in ancient times, when many enemies had been killed in war, people would grieve for them and pity them for dying on the battlefield, and the victorious side would even hold funerals for the fallen. As for enemies who surrendered and came over, one should all the more pity, reassure and exhort them. If one kills enemies who have already surrendered and submitted, such a heart is truly too cruel and ruthless, and the evil karma created is also too great; so the calamity one will meet in the future is greater than any other!

Mr. Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty said: ‘A person with a heavy heart of compassion cannot lead troops to fight as a general! Does it mean that being a general is a road to certain death? Not so. If a general can save the people, quell upheaval and bring stability to the state, then being a general has a road to life. Therefore, because one saves the multitudes and kills only when one cannot help it, then no merit is greater than a general’s. Why? Because sacrificing a few lives to save tens of millions of lives is of course different from ordinary acts of virtue. If, in order to accomplish one’s own fame and merit, one uses slaughter to harm living beings, then no guilt is greater than a general’s. Why? Because if one loses a battle one kills many of one’s own troops, and if one wins a battle one kills many of the enemy’s troops; and if military discipline is not strict, one will recklessly slaughter innocent civilians — all of this is the responsibility of the commanding general! Therefore the appointment of a general must not be taken lightly; and the general’s appointment of his subordinates is especially something that must not be taken lightly! The ancients said: “To be a general for three generations is what the Daoists regard as taboo.” However, using killing to put an end to killing is also an unavoidable matter, but can it be done with ease of mind? Therefore in dispatching and employing generals, one must observe the following three prohibitions. First, one fears initiating trouble where there is none, sacrificing the lives of a million soldiers in order to gain for oneself the seal of a feudal lord. Second, one fears replacing violence with even greater violence, slaughtering innocent civilians and cutting off more heads in order to compete for merit. Third, one fears exhausting and bitter fighting between the two armies, each killing many of the other’s troops. Those who personally undertake this combat mission will say: “Killing is up to me — in this way the goal of establishing authority can be achieved!” They will also say: “Killing is done by others — I let them recklessly slaughter and plunder, bluffing and posturing, and then I may take that as my own combat merit!” One should know that the most important thing in the way of a general is to strictly forbid the army to kill; and with strict governance of the troops the soldiers will not be harmed and will be able to accomplish merit in whatever direction they advance. This is the principle of carrying out killing by means of the way of life!’

The great Han general Li Guang, skilled in martial arts and excellent in archery, was greatly feared by the Xiongnu, and so Li Guang was called the Flying General. The great Tang poet Wang Changling wrote a poem on the frontier, praising Li Guang’s valor, saying: ‘The bright moon of Qin and the passes of Han; those who set forth on the ten-thousand-li march have not yet returned. If only the Flying General of Dragon City were here, the barbarian horses would never cross the Yinshan Mountains.’ However, Li Guang’s official fortune was poor: though his military merit was outstanding, he was never able to obtain a noble title. Li Guang once said to the physiognomist Wang Shuo: ‘Since I, Li Guang, joined the army in my youth, in every battle with the Xiongnu I have never failed to be first, risking my life to kill the enemy and win merit. Whenever Han troops pursued the Xiongnu, I always participated. Yet those younger than I who joined the army later have all been enfeoffed; while I alone remain unenfeoffed. What is the reason for this?’ Wang Shuo said: ‘General, please think carefully — in your whole life, is there anything that you have done that makes you feel regret?’ Li Guang replied: ‘I once killed eight hundred surrendered barbarians, and afterward I deeply regretted it.’ Wang Shuo said: ‘No calamity is greater than killing enemies who have already surrendered. This is the reason you cannot be enfeoffed.’ Later, when Li Guang marched against the Xiongnu, he lost his way in the desert, and Li Guang took his own life in despair. His grandson Li Ling also became a general, and in one battle was captured and surrendered to the Xiongnu; and so Li Ling’s family, by imperial decree of the Han emperor, was beheaded in a mass execution.
